title: 4 days, Claude + ChatGPT + Tripo, a co-op 3D browser hack-and-slash. What worked, what didn't, and the numbers so far
author: FeedbackHaunting5261
selftext:
I have been building Rift Hunter for four days. It is a 3D hack-and-slash roguelite in three.js that runs in the browser, with four weapon classes, 4-player co-op, 1v1 duels and a lobby chat. Free, no install. https://\[redacted\]-ops.itch.io/three-gates-night

  
The split of work. Claude writes all the code. ChatGPT makes the 2D art and Tripo makes the 3D models. I decide what gets built, play it, and reject things.

  
What worked

  
Telling the agent to assume there are bugs and audit everything before a release. That framing found far more than asking it to check its work.

  
Letting the agent play the game. For the co-op build it opened four browser tabs with four accounts, formed a party and ran three gates. That is how we caught a downed-player notice showing twice and two identical runes drawing as two slots.

  
Small checkers in the repo. One script fails if any Korean string has no English entry, another flags undeclared or unused names. The agent runs them every time, so regressions stay cheap.

  
No game server for co-op. Players join an MQTT topic by party code and the host's browser simulates the monsters. Good enough for four players and costs nothing to run.

  
What did not work

  
The first cover and tagline. They described settings instead of the game, and the itch click-through sat at 0.2 percent over about 2,400 impressions. Both are replaced now, too early to say if it helped.

  
The first minute. About half of new players close the tab inside the first room, between 16 and 66 seconds in. I could not tell from the logs whether that is frame rate or people not finding the attack button, so today's build records average fps, touch or not, kills and input count per run.

  
If you try it, the thing I most want to know is how the first room felt on your machine.

replies.body: "Do you use an iPhone? I've tested it on phones several times, and they were all Galaxies, though..."

replies.author: Beneficial_Feed_2595
replies.body:
I have an iPhone.  
It still doesn’t work. It gets stuck on the turn or landscape mode bit.

replies.author: FeedbackHaunting5261
replies.body:
Thanks, that told me exactly where it broke. A web page can't rotate the screen on an iPhone, so with rotation lock on you were stuck on that prompt forever. I just pushed v0.8.16: the prompt is gone and the game draws itself sideways when the phone is upright, so it should start whichever way you hold it.

Same link, just reload: https://ugiomin31-ops.itch.io/three-gates-night

If you get a minute to try again, I'd like to know whether it gets past the title screen now.

replies.author: FeedbackHaunting5261
replies.body:
Sorry, that was on me. The link in the post was broken, so it would not have opened on anything. Fixed now: https://ugiomin31-ops.itch.io/three-gates-night 

It has touch controls and should run in a phone browser in landscape. If it still fails for you, which phone and browser?

comments.author: Beneficial_Feed_2595
comments.body:
A few notes as to why I bounced off almost right away.

1.) Continually having to press to swing the sword was annoying.  
2.) zero story or asthetic hook— am I just in a while hallway swinging at green men why?  
3.) enemies took forever to kill.

No real positive reason for me to keep playing. I like vampire survivors for reference. Oh and this audio being ai generated repeating was what really did it.

I wouldn’t play this game. No gameplay reward and now music or visual or story to keep me hooked. Nothing to make me want to keep exploring.

replies.author: FeedbackHaunting5261
replies.body:
Glad it runs now, and thank you for writing out why you quit. That list was more useful than anything in my logs, so I spent the afternoon on it:

1. You never had to tap. Holding the button keeps swinging, but nothing told you that. The attack button now blinks with a HOLD tag until you have actually held it.

2. Enemies in the first gate now die in two or three hits, and the first level-up lands after about ten kills instead of after the whole room.

3. The white hallway is gone. Half the lamps are dead, part of the ceiling has come down, the floor is cracked and there is a red emergency light at the far end.

4. The music was a 30-second loop, which is why it grated. The subway track is two minutes now and quieter. The other gates still have short loops and are next.

No story hook yet beyond a two-line intro, and that is a fair hit. Since you like Vampire Survivors: would auto-attack have kept you in, or was it mostly the lack of a reason to keep going?

comments.author: biggdogg420
comments.body: The new HOLD label gives you a useful event to measure. I’d compare three milestones for the first room: attempted attack, first hit landed, first level-up. If people leave before attempting, look at controls. If they attack but never hit, look at targeting or feedback. If they reach a level-up and still leave, watch whether the reward gives them a reason to try the next room.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
The first-minute drop is worth chasing before anything else. In my mobile game half of all runs end inside 19 seconds, and for a long time I couldn't tell bad luck from confusion either.

Two things helped. Recording per-run inputs like you're about to do: a run with almost no input is someone who didn't find the controls, and that's a different fix from someone who fought and died. And changing what a brand new player lands in. I had been opening the game on the online mode for first-timers, and moved them to the simplest mode instead.

On letting the agent play: agreed, it finds real bugs. One caution from my side is that a bot reacts instantly and never hesitates, so it told me the difficulty was fine when real people were struggling. For anything about how hard the first room feels, I had to build a deliberately slower, sloppier test player.

replies.author: FeedbackHaunting5261
replies.body:
Thanks, both of these turned into changes today.

The run record only had a total input count, so I split it into attacks, skill casts, dodges and seconds spent moving, plus how long until the first attack. That should separate "never found the controls" from "fought and left".

The slower test player was the bigger one. I built one that reacts late, aims off, pauses, rarely uses skills and never goes looking for an objective. The first room was fine. The second room asks you to kill two summoners and keeps sending packs until you do, and all three versions of the sloppy player just fought the packs until they ran out of revives, one of them after 860 kills. My normal bots never showed it because they walk straight to the target. The one real player I have a record for since the last update quit in that same room after 119 kills.

So in the first gate the packs now stop after 30 seconds and only the summoners are left. Same test players closed the gate in 8 of 9 runs after that. Whether real people do is the next thing to watch.
